name: thread-safe-copy-on-write
intent: Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see.
problem: A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing table, registry, cache snapshot - that must be read without locking and updated by cloning.
context: Applies where one object, or one immutable snapshot of an aggregate, is read by many threads and written rarely: configuration reloads, registries and symbol tables, caches with rare invalidation, listener registries, and large immutable values handed between threads. Manual memory management, non-atomic reference counts or a separate publication step make the problem sharpest (C, C++, hand-rolled counting); garbage-collected languages apply the same structure with the published reference replacing the count. It is an object/value-level data-sharing decision, not a lock strategy for write-heavy state.
benefits: Readers never block and never acquire a lock: they load the published snapshot once, in one atomic step, and work on it, so read throughput scales with cores instead of serialising on a mutex.
Copies stay cheap while the value is shared: cloning a handle is one counter increment or one pointer load, and the deep copy is deferred until the value actually diverges.
Readers get a consistent snapshot: a writer publishes a whole new body, so a reader sees either the old version or the new one, never a half-updated structure.
Readers and writers stop disturbing each other's cache lines: only writers touch the shared coordination state, so a read-mostly workload no longer bounces a lock or a counter between cores.
Failure containment: a writer that fails or rejects an update simply does not publish, leaving the previous snapshot intact for every reader.
The write path is explicit and local - clone, modify the clone, publish once - which makes the mutation sequence easy to serialise, review and test.
tradeoffs: Every write pays the full price of a copy plus publication; under a write-heavy workload the pattern is strictly worse than a lock, turning waiting into O(n) copying and garbage.
Publication is atomic, transactions are not: concurrent read-modify-write loses updates unless writers share a mutex or a compare-and-swap retry loop, and even then the update is not a transaction.

Readers must pin their snapshot for the whole logical read: any reference - iterator, raw pointer, borrowed view - that outlives the publish point keeps the old body alive, so a real reclamation discipline is required (ownership of a counted reference, hazard pointers or epochs, or a garbage collector).

Protecting the count is not protecting the publication: a plain pointer read while a writer swaps it is still a data race, so the safe form publishes the pointer atomically as well; 'the count is atomic' is not enough.

Value semantics become non-obvious: two handles look like independent values but share a body, and any leaked interior reference - a non-const operator[], a shallow copy of a nested object, a mutable element inside an 'immutable' snapshot - voids the copy-on-write barrier silently.
Contention is invisible: clone-and-retry loops never block, so a badly balanced workload quietly burns CPU on discarded copies instead of showing up as lock wait.
Memory overhead: every published generation is a full body, and in reference-counted languages cycles pin bodies forever unless back-edges are weak.

participants.responsibility: Cheap value-like handle that owns a reference to the body; copying it shares the body, and mutating through it detaches (clones) first.
The shared payload. Once published it is treated as immutable; a writer replaces it rather than mutating it in place.
The reference count and/or the published pointer - exactly the state the thread-safe variant must protect atomically instead of by mutual exclusion.
Loads the current body in one atomic step, holds its reference for the whole operation, and never locks.
Serialises with other writers, clones the snapshot it loaded, applies the change and publishes the new body in one store or compare-and-swap.
Decides when a replaced body's last reference is gone - the atomic count reaching zero, the last owning handle dropping, or the collector collecting it - and returns the memory.

use_cases: Read-mostly configuration or routing tables that are reloaded occasionally and read on every request by every worker thread.
Registries, symbol tables and interning tables built once and consulted constantly, with rare additions or invalidations.
Caches and memo tables where invalidation is rare and readers must never wait behind a writer.
Listener and observer registries traversed on every event and modified rarely - the classic CopyOnWriteArrayList use.
Large immutable values - strings, byte buffers, message payloads, compiled artefacts - handed between threads, where a deep copy at each hand-off would dominate.
Language runtimes, interpreters and plugin hosts that keep configuration or environment objects read by many threads and updated by a single owner.

The Linux kernel's RCU (read-copy-update) mechanism in its purest form: readers enter an rcu_read_lock() critical section with no lock, atomic or shared-memory write, updaters publish a replacement with rcu_assign_pointer(), and the superseded body is freed only after a grace period proves no reader can still hold it - the dentry cache, routing tables and network-device lists.

Rust's std::sync::Arc as the atomically counted body of the standard library: cloning an Arc increments the count, and Arc::make_mut detaches - cloning the inner value only when other Arc handles exist - so the sharing state is protected by the type rather than by convention.

Go services publishing an immutable configuration or routing snapshot through sync/atomic's atomic.Pointer[T]: readers Load it once per request without locking, writers build a fresh snapshot under a writer lock and Store or Swap the pointer, and the collector reclaims each superseded snapshot when no reader references it.
avoid_when: Writes are not rare: a plain mutex or read-write lock around a mutable body is less machinery and less copying, because copy-per-write is O(n) per update.
The value is already deeply immutable: share it directly; no count or publication protocol is needed when nothing can mutate it.

The runtime already removes the sharing problem (actors/workers with message passing, or collections that are persistent by default): use message passing or a persistent data structure instead of a counted body.

Readers cannot hold a reference for the whole operation (they keep raw pointers or iterators into the body): use a lock, or an RCU-like protocol with an explicit grace period, instead of a count nobody owns.
The value is small enough that copying it is cheaper than the coordination (small strings, small structs): just copy it.

The platform already ships the pattern for your shape of data (java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList, .NET System.Collections.Immutable, persistent collections): use those rather than a hand-rolled counted handle.
anti_patterns: A hand-rolled copy-on-write handle whose reference count is a plain integer touched from several threads: increments get lost, bodies are freed while another thread reads them, or they leak.
Protecting the count but not the publication: dereferencing a shared pointer that another thread replaces - an atomic count does not make the pointer swap safe.

Handing out an interior reference into the shared body (an operator[] returning a writable reference, a mutable nested object inside an 'immutable' snapshot), so a reader mutates a snapshot every other reader sees.
Copying on every write in a write-heavy path with no batching or bound: the pattern degenerates into an allocation storm and the lock it replaced starts looking cheap.
Concurrent read-modify-write with no writer serialisation: two writers clone the same snapshot and one update is silently lost - copy-on-write gives atomic publication, not atomic updates.

Using copy-on-write to avoid deciding who owns the data: replaced bodies stay alive because a handle, iterator or registry still references them, and in reference-counted languages cycles pin them forever.
design_principles: Prefer immutability for shared state: readers of an immutable body need no synchronisation; only publication needs an atomic step.
Separate the read path from the write path: readers never block and writers never disturb readers - an asymmetric, RCU-like discipline.
Make the sharing state part of the type, not a convention: the count or the published pointer lives in the handle/control block so no caller can forget it.
Lazy copy: pay for divergence, not for sharing - copy-on-write is lazy initialisation applied to copying.
Encapsulate the barrier: only the handle may detach or republish, and the body must not leak a mutation path around it.
Ownership must be explicit: every handle owns exactly one reference, and every replaced body has a defined last owner.
best_practices: Make the count atomic and the publication atomic: use the language's atomic reference-counted pointer (std::shared_ptr with std::atomic<std::shared_ptr>, Rust Arc, C11 _Atomic) or an atomically published reference (AtomicReference, atomic.Pointer, ImmutableInterlocked) - never a bare integer incremented by two threads.
Serialise writers around clone-and-publish: clone the snapshot you loaded, mutate the clone, publish once (mutex or CAS retry loop); never mutate the body after publication.
Load the snapshot once into a local and hold it for the whole logical read - never read the handle twice for parts of one consistent view.
Batch updates: apply a group of changes to one clone and publish once, so the copy cost is paid per transaction rather than per field.
Keep the body deeply immutable (freeze the leaves, store immutable values) so nothing can route around the barrier.

Give replaced bodies a way to die: drop references promptly, use weak references for back-edges and registries in reference-counted languages, and pair manual memory with an explicit hand-off discipline (hazard pointers or epochs).
Prefer the platform's implementation when it exists (CopyOnWriteArrayList, System.Collections.Immutable, Arc::make_mut, persistent collections) and hand-roll only for the shape it does not cover.
Measure the write rate before adopting: if writes are not rare, use a lock - copy-on-write is a read-path optimisation.
sources: More C++ Idioms (Wikibooks): 'Copy-on-write' and 'Thread-safe Copy-on-write' - the catalogue entry this record materializes; the first documents the reference-counted body with detach-on-write and its unshareable-flag pitfall (citing Sutter), the second the atomic-snapshot form with mutex-serialized writers: https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Thread-safe_Copy-on-write
Herb Sutter, More Exceptional C++ (Addison-Wesley, 2002), Items 13-16 - the copy-on-write string analysis and the unshareable fix for interior references, cited by the Copy-on-write idiom page.

GCC libstdc++ manual, Dual ABI - the C++11 conformance change that 'forbids Copy-On-Write strings', replacing libstdc++'s COW std::string in GCC 5.1: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/libstdc++/manual/using_dual_abi.html

cppreference, std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> - the shared_ptr control block is thread-safe for distinct shared_ptr objects, but unsynchronized access to the same shared_ptr object is a data race: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/shared_ptr/atomic2

Paul E. McKenney, 'What is RCU? - Read, Copy, Update' (Linux kernel documentation) - the canonical definition of the lock-free-read / copy / update / deferred-reclaim split this pattern generalises: https://docs.kernel.org/RCU/whatisRCU.html

Linux kernel documentation, 'RCU Concepts' - grace-period reclamation: remove the reference first, free only after synchronize_rcu()/call_rcu() proves all pre-existing readers finished, and why RCU read sides use no locks, atomics or shared-memory writes: https://docs.kernel.org/RCU/rcu.html

Oracle Java SE documentation, java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList - mutative ops copy the whole backing array and iterators traverse a fixed snapshot: the GC-language realisation of this pattern and its own 'avoid when writes are frequent' warning: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/CopyOnWriteArrayList.html

Rust standard library documentation, std::sync::Arc - atomic reference counting across threads, with Arc::make_mut implementing detach-on-write by cloning the inner value only when other handles exist: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html
Go documentation, sync/atomic - atomic.Pointer[T] (Go 1.19+) with Load/Store/Swap/CompareAndSwap for lock-free publication and replacement of immutable snapshots: https://pkg.go.dev/sync/atomic

javamex, 'Copy-on-write collections in Java' - the misuse analysis: reads cost a volatile read and never block, but writes are serialised and each pays a full-array copy, so the structure degrades into an allocation storm under write load: https://www.javamex.com/tutorials/synchronization_concurrency_8_copy_on_write.shtml
